Joe Skipper | Reuters After a booster explosion on Friday, SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday — a triumphant milestone for the company. SpaceX made the historic catch using its "chopsticks," mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its facility in Starbase, Texas. Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship test yet, marked the first time Musk's company attempted to catch both the rocket's booster and upper stage. During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water. The rocket's upper stage then continued into orbit and flew around the Earth 14 times before successfully landing on SpaceX's launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla. The Hawaii Department of Transportation issued a temporary pause on some West Coast flights Friday, due to debris risk from the flight. Separately, the FAA issued a rare, nationwide ground stop due to telecommunications system failures. (Both of those orders have since been lifted.) Making Starship a reliable and fully reusable rocket is critical to SpaceX's ambitions. In the near term, the company needs Starship to send more satellites into orbit to expand its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center. SpaceX is also expected to use Starship to bring astronauts and cargo from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and back for NASA . Musk also has a grand vision to use Starship to "colonize Mars" and "make humanity multi-planetary." During Test Flight 15 on Friday, SpaceX released another 26 of its newest Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, growing its commercial satellite internet network. The authority also said that it had reserved the right to assess separately a new feature, launched in 2026, that allows content from users' galleries to be processed in the cloud. headlines.article_text: Ground stop followed contractor upgrade to L3Harris telecom system: Duffy Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Flight disruptions continued into the weekend as airlines raced to recover from the FAA's nationwide ground stop. The ground stop came after updates to an older communication system managed by L3Harris Technologies, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The disruption forced sports teams to make alternative travel arrangements, with some college football games postponed. In this article AAL LHX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy (R) speaks alongside FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford (L) during a press briefing at the Department of Transportation headquarters building in Washington, DC, on November 14, 2026. Aaron Schwartz | Afp | Getty Images The longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 came after updates to a telecommunications system made by L3Harris Technologies , Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday, as travel disruptions lingered for thousands of passengers nationwide. There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference. The updates were part of ongoing work of switching from a copper wire system to fiberoptic cable, Duffy said. When a router was switched to fiberoptic cable from copper, it had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, Duffy said, creating problems with airplane communications and radar feeds. Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports. "We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. L3Harris didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. Duffy told the press conference that the FAA is investigating. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said. Flight disruptions linger Flight disruptions continued on Saturday. More than 3,700 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and close to 2,000 were delayed as of 9:40 a.m. ET, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of about 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather. Part of untangling from the ground stop includes getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports. Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period. Airlines offer crews extra pay American Airlines , for example, is offering flight attendants extra pay to pick up trips, according to a person familiar with the airline's plans.
